title: CTS 2026 Weekly Survey 01 - Divorce and Remarriage
privacy_note: This file contains aggregate public results only. Names, email addresses, response identifiers, respondent-level records, and raw free-text suggestions are excluded.

update_policy.note: This preliminary report will be refreshed each Tuesday morning while the survey remains open. It may also be refreshed sooner if new responses materially change the results. A final report should be stamped after the response window closes and the SurveyOL export is reviewed.

items.text: In ordinary cases, a spouse's sexual adultery constitutes biblically legitimate grounds for divorce.
In ordinary cases, a spouse's persistent physical abuse constitutes biblically legitimate grounds for divorce even if sexual adultery has not occurred.
In ordinary cases, a spouse's severe and persistent emotional or psychological abuse can constitute biblically legitimate grounds for divorce.
In ordinary cases, willful abandonment by an unbelieving spouse constitutes biblically legitimate grounds for divorce.
In ordinary cases, a spouse's persistent pornography use can become biblically legitimate grounds for divorce.
In ordinary cases, a spouse's romantic but nonsexual infidelity can constitute biblically legitimate grounds for divorce.
A Christian whose divorce was biblically legitimate is normally free to remarry.
Churches should normally require pastoral review before affirming the remarriage of a divorced Christian.
Churches should use formal discipline when members knowingly pursue a biblically illegitimate divorce.
In my ministry context, churches are generally too permissive about divorce and remarriage.
Churches should treat immediate physical safety as a priority before pursuing marital reconciliation in abusive marriages.
Pastors should distinguish carefully between ordinary marital conflict and patterns of coercive control when counseling about divorce.
Pastors should sometimes name specific political movements or parties when warning a congregation about moral compromise.
Churches should encourage regular fasting as a normal expectation for mature Christian discipleship.
Churches should avoid using worship songs from ministries whose leaders teach serious doctrinal error, even when the songs themselves are orthodox.
A church should require formal membership before a person serves in any public ministry role.
Pastors should normally mention specific false teachers by name when their teachings are influencing the congregation.
Christians should avoid recreational marijuana use even where it is legal.
Christian parents should consider a school's moral and religious formation more important than its academic quality.
Churches should publicly repent for institutional failures even when current leaders were not personally involved.
Pastors should avoid platforming guest speakers whose doctrine differs from the church on secondary issues.
A church should refuse to host community events sponsored by groups that publicly oppose Christian sexual ethics.

next_week_ballot_draft.note: Five items are polished from participant suggestions. Two items are carried over from the Week 1 participant ballot because they ranked highest there.

items.text: Christians are morally obligated to disobey civil laws that require them to violate clear biblical commands.
Churches should teach explicitly on the moral and pastoral implications of IVF and other assisted reproductive technologies.
Women should be permitted to serve in any church ministry role for which they are spiritually gifted and otherwise qualified.
Baptism should ordinarily precede participation in the Lord's Supper.
Churches should teach Christians how to use artificial intelligence faithfully and critically as part of contemporary discipleship.
A church should require formal membership before a person serves in any public ministry role.
Pastors should normally mention specific false teachers by name when their teachings are influencing the congregation.
